Ever since U.S. President Donald Trump began his second term in office, his administration’s
conduct of foreign policy has been that of a schoolyard bully. This is particularly true in 2026,
when the U.S. launched attacks on two oil-rich countries, Venezuela and Iran. The first was on the
blatantly false pretext of terming President Nicolás Maduro the head of a drug cartel, and the
second was at the instance of Israel. As with schoolyard bullies everywhere, the Trump
administration recognises no rules and mistakes the absence of violent resistance for proof of its
strength. The strangling of Cuba is a case in point. After seizing Venezuela’s energy assets,
abducting its President, and cutting off Venezuelan oil supply to Havana, the U.S. threatened
countries such as Mexico that sought to step into the breach, and imposed a de facto naval blockade
on Cuba, leading to a severe fuel crunch and acute distress for ordinary Cubans. This behaviour,
justified by Mr. Trump as an attempt to take over Cuba and remove its decades-long communist
government, is part of a strategy so nakedly imperial that it has been termed the “Donroe Doctrine”,
a crude play on the original instrument of U.S. hemispheric dominance for over two centuries. Yet,
the bully’s power is often brittle and holds only until someone calls the bluff. When Russia, Cuba’s
ally since the Soviet era, dispatched a tanker, Anatoly Kolodkin, as humanitarian aid to fuel-
starved Cuba, it also tested the will of the Trump administration to interdict a ship owned by
another nuclear power. The tanker reached without incident.


The U.S., it turns out, did not push back and the bluff now stands exposed, even if by a country
that has itself displayed similar behaviour in neighbouring Ukraine. Cuba’s fuel crisis has not
ended and the threat of American attacks still hangs over the socialist government led by President
Miguel Díaz-Canel. But Russia’s timely help reveals that the rest of the world need not simply
endure the Trump era as this administration goes about breaking every accepted tenet of the
international order. For all its flaws as a one-party state, Cuba has been an avowed member of the
Non-Aligned Movement, has shown solidarity with the Global South by deploying well-trained
doctors for medical programmes across poor countries, and has contributed materially to anti-
colonial struggles for decades. It is time other countries repaid the Cubans by showing the will to
break the American blockade and continue sovereign trade and commerce with Cuba, asserting

Idleness, vice, and intemperance had done their miserable work, and the dead mother lay cold
and still amid her wretched children. She had fallen upon the threshold of her own door in a
drunken fit, and died in the presence of her frightened little ones. Neighbors went hastily to the old
tumble-down hut, in which she had secured little more than a place of shelter from summer heats
and winter cold: some with grave-clothes for a decent interment of the body; and some with food

for the half-starving children, three in number. Of these, John, the oldest, a boy of twelve, was a
stout lad, able to earn his living with any farmer. Kate, between ten and eleven, was a bright, active
girl, out of whom something clever might be made, if in good hands; but poor little Maggie, the
youngest, was hopelessly diseased. Two years before a fall from a window had injured her spine,
and she had not been able to leave her bed since, except when lifted in the arms of her mother.


"What is to be done with the children?" That was the chief question now. The dead mother would
go underground, and be forever beyond all care or concern of the villagers. But the children must
not be left to starve. After considering the matter, and talking it over with his wife, farmer Jones
said that he would take John, and do well by him, now that his mother was out of the way; and
Mrs. Ellis, who had been looking out for a bound girl, concluded that it would be charitable in her
to make choice of Katy, even though she was too young to be of much use for several years.


"I could do much better, I know," said Mrs. Ellis; "but as no one seems inclined to take her, I must
act from a sense of duty. I expect to have trouble with the child; for she's an undisciplined thing--
used to having her own way."


But no one said "I'll take Maggie." Pitying glances were cast on her wan and wasted form and
thoughts were troubled on her account. Mothers brought cast-off garments and, removing her
soiled and ragged clothes, dressed her in clean attire. The sad eyes and patient face of the little
one touched many hearts, and even knocked at them for entrance. But none opened to take her in.
Who wanted a bed-ridden child?


"Take her to the poorhouse," said a rough man, of whom the question "What's to be done with
Maggie?" was asked. "Nobody's going to be bothered with her."

It might be difficult to imagine today but just two decades ago, the Maoist movement held large
swathes of central and eastern India in its grip. Roughly a fourth of India’s districts had seen Left-
wing extremism in some form, and chunks of its tribal heartland were under the writ of the
insurgency. Though Naxalism first took root in the north Bengal hills in the 1970s amid simmering
peasant unrest and anxiety about economic inequality, a hungrier and more violent Maoist
ideology had slowly spread across central India in the 1990s, reaching its peak in the 2000s and
2010s. Even after prime minister Manmohan Singh described Maoism as India’s biggest internal
security challenge in 2006, the insurgency only gained in strength, inflicting severe infrastructure
damage and conducting a string of attacks that resulted in the deaths of hundreds of civilians and
security personnel. An ill-advised attempt to create a citizen’s militia against the rebels only ended
up antagonising the tribal population while committing human rights violations.


It is against this grim historical backdrop that the spectacle of Maoism on its last legs looks
impressive. Union home minister Amit Shah on Monday told Parliament that the government had
met its March 31, 2026 deadline to weed out Left-wing extremism in the country, underling this
administration’s tougher, more muscular stance against the insurgent — bullet for bullet. The home
minister rightly praised the government’s efforts to make infrastructure inroads into regions once
deemed impenetrable — erecting mobile phone towers, building roads and markets, and
establishing police outposts. But once the Maoists are wiped out, the government will need to
redouble its efforts, both on security arrangements and civilian administration.


At the heart of the Maoist success was a kernel of discontent among ordinary people who felt
abandoned by the administration, especially in moments of tragedy or disaster. A credible and
transparent civilian administration with fair elections that ensures the active participation of local
communities, must remain high on the agenda of the authorities. This will require a change of
gears — from a muscular securitised approach to a softer, more humane, more democratic one.
Authorities must stay away from heavy handed operations or building local militias; instead they
must bolster law and order. Corruption and apathy — often the bane of civic authorities elsewhere

It is not for nothing that the head of Art Recovery International has lamented the current “smash
and grab period” of art thievery. The masked men who broke into the Magnani Rocca Foundation
in Italy’s Parma region and made off with three paintings — a Renoir, a Cézanne and a Matisse
— showed little patience for the finesse and style that seem to have characterised such endeavours
in the past. They used a crowbar to force open an entrance and were in and out in under three
minutes.


Gentlemen thieves like Thomas Crown and Arsène Lupin may be mere products of the
imagination, but art history is replete with stories of purloiners who combined their taste for the
rare and beautiful — and the profits they bring — with a sense of mischief and real love for the
art. Take the two Norwegian burglars who stole Edvard Munch’s “The Scream” from the National

with 13 works.


Then there was Stéphane Breitwieser, art thief extraordinaire who walked off with pieces from
nearly 200 museums — simply because they moved him. No smashed glass, hold-ups or bloodshed
were involved, just good taste and chutzpah. His luck turned in 2001 when his mother, angered by
his criminal behaviour, disposed of his nearly $1.25-billion collection, and Breitwieser was
arrested. The smashers-and-grabbers of today may not execute their crimes with quite the same
insouciance or love, but their desire to turn their loot to profit at least keeps alive the hope that
someday the priceless works will be found and restored.

India is fast becoming one of the world’s biggest AI user bases. The question now is how it can
turn that scale into superpower status rather than just training Silicon Valley for free. That will be
a tall order for a country largely caught flat-footed by the boom. But let’s start with the basics: The
three main building blocks of AI are talent, compute (including high-end chips and infrastructure)
and data. India doesn’t lack engineers, but it currently lacks foundational research training at scale


Head Office: Building No.6, Opp. Mio Coworks, Saidulajab, Saket, New Delhi – 110030           12minutestoclat.com

and sufficient advanced processors in public labs and universities. What it has, in abundance, is
data. It should treat this as a strategic asset rather than leaking it as a free export.


It’s a key reason US Big Tech is making a blitz for the market. With roughly a billion people
online and a massive mobile-first population, India generates a torrent of the kind of human
feedback that makes AI systems better on a daily basis. The world’s most-populous country is the
second-biggest user base of both OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude after the US, while
accounting for just a fraction of these platforms’ revenue. The dynamic exposes how much more
the market matters for training purposes right now than making money. These free-to-use services
and promotions aimed at Indian phone users come with a cost. It’s part of a strategic Silicon Valley
grab for Indian languages, voices and behaviours that will make foreign systems smarter first. The
South Asian nation risks repeating a familiar historical pattern of exporting the raw materials for
pennies then buying back imported models at a premium. Meanwhile, it will be left to absorb a job
shock and social impacts at home.


Ultimately, India’s data reckoning should be about who controls this strategic input to AI and who
captures the value from it. The answer isn’t to wall off user outputs from the world. It’s about
finding creative solutions and leveraging them to set rules that reflect what’s actually being
extracted. If its peoples’ data is a key ingredient for building advanced AI, the government should
demand more than apps and marketing in return. It can seek partnerships that build capacity,
including public compute commitments, access to high-end chips, robust training pipelines for AI
researchers, and collaborations that go beyond token commitments.

The programme of “non-violent non-cooperation” included the boycott of councils, courts and
schools, set up by the British and of all foreign cloth. With some naivete Gandhi claimed that his
movement was not unconstitutional: in his dictionary, constitutional and moral were synonymous
terms. The British saw that the success of “non-cooperation” would paralyse their administration,
Lord Chelmsford, the Viceroy, tried to kill with ridicule ‘the most foolish of all foolish schemes”,
which would “bring ruin to those who had any stake in the country”. A number of eminent
“moderate’ politicians joined official critics in underlining the risks of mass non-cooperation as
proposed by Gandhi. That a political programme had no chance of success without an adequate
organization to implement it, Gandhi had realized at the age of twenty-five, when he had founded
the Natal Indian Congress to fight for the rights of Indians in Natal. The Indian National Congress,
had, therefore, to be refashioned, if it was to prove an efficient instrument of non-violent non-
cooperation, Gandhi saw that what the country needed was not a forum for an annual pageant and
feast of oratory, but a militant organization in touch with the masses. Under the new constitution,
the congress was given a broad-based pyramidal structure by formation of village, taluka, district
and provincial committees, with the All India Congress Committee and the Working committee at

Consideration turns a bare promise into an enforceable obligation. Section 2(d) of the Indian
Contract Act, 1872 treats any act, abstinence or promise furnished at the desire of the promisor as
sufficient consideration, and Section 25 renders an agreement without consideration void as a
general rule, subject to three carve outs. First, a promise founded on natural love and affection
between parties standing in a near relationship binds the promisor only if the promise is committed
to writing and registered. Second, a promise to compensate a person who has already, on their own
initiative, rendered some service to the promisor may be enforced even though the service preceded
the promise. Third, a written and signed promise to discharge a debt that has become unenforceable

through the passage of time will bind the promisor notwithstanding the absence of fresh

Distinct from consideration is the rule that only those who are parties to a bargain may sue upon
it. English authority anchored this proposition in a dispute over the resale price of tyres, and Indian
courts, though never codifying the rule in statute, have consistently declined to let outsiders
enforce agreements made for their advantage. Yet courts carve narrow inlets through this wall. A
person named as the object of a trust may compel its performance despite standing outside the
contract that created it. A family settlement drawn up to benefit a relative allows that relative to
insist on its terms even without having signed the settlement. Where a charge is fastened onto
immovable property for the benefit of a third person, that person too may enforce the charge.
Courts have repeatedly cautioned against widening this list further; each addition has demanded
proof that the arrangement was unmistakably designed to confer a direct benefit on the outsider,
and mere incidental advantage will not suffice to displace the general bar against strangers suing
on a contract.

Article 352 whenever the security of India, or any part of it, is threatened by war, external
aggression or armed rebellion. The last ground replaced the older, more elastic phrase internal
disturbance through the Forty Fourth Amendment of 1978, a change meant to raise the threshold
for invoking this power. Before such a proclamation can issue, the Cabinet must tender its advice
in writing; the proclamation must secure approval from both Houses of Parliament, by a majority

A proclaimed emergency reshapes the ordinarily federal distribution of legislative and executive

India has invoked this power three times, in 1962 during hostilities with China, in 1971 during the

mandatory written Cabinet advice, a strict one month window for parliamentary ratification, and
revocability by an ordinary Lok Sabha majority, were direct responses to that experience. The
Supreme Court has since clarified, in a 1980 ruling upholding the basic structure against a
sweeping amendment, that courts retain some capacity to examine the validity of an emergency
proclamation, rather than treating it as wholly beyond judicial reach.

The Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 embodies a beneficial scheme under which compensation for
accident victims must be just, adequate and calculated to restore the claimant, so far as money can,
to the position enjoyed before the accident. Tribunals compute this compensation under two broad
limbs: pecuniary loss, principally the loss of dependency or of the estate calculated from the
deceased or injured person's income, and non pecuniary loss, comprising conventional heads such
as loss of consortium, loss of estate, and funeral or transportation expenses. The Supreme Court
has periodically standardised these conventional heads to prevent wide disparity between tribunals
awarding compensation for materially similar losses.

Where an injury rather than death is involved, the assessment does not stop at the percentage of
physical disability certified by a medical board. Courts have long distinguished physical disability,
a clinical measurement, from functional disability, which asks how far the injury actually impairs
the claimant's capacity to pursue the specific vocation by which she earned her livelihood. A
claimant whose profession depends on a particular physical capability may suffer a functional loss
far exceeding the certified physical percentage, and tribunals must examine the claimant's
occupation, skill and future prospects rather than mechanically applying the certified figure.

Consortium too has expanded beyond its historical confines. What began as a spouse's claim for
loss of companionship has been read to extend to comparable claims by parents for the loss of a
child's care and by children for the loss of a parent's guidance, each recognised as a distinct
conventional head payable in addition to, and not in substitution for, pecuniary loss. Tribunals
retain a continuing obligation to identify heads of loss that legitimately arise on the facts before
them, even where a particular head was not specifically pressed by the claimant or awarded by the
court below.

The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 preserves a graded scheme of property offences inherited from
the earlier Penal Code. Theft, defined under Section 303, consists of dishonestly taking movable
property out of another's possession without that person's consent. Two elements are
indispensable: the property must be movable, so that machinery or fixtures become capable of
theft only once severed from the earth, and the taking must be both dishonest and without the
possessor's consent. The offence is complete the moment the property is moved with dishonest
intent, irrespective of whether the offender ultimately succeeds in carrying it away.

Extortion, defined under Section 308, dispenses with the requirement of a surreptitious taking
altogether. It is committed when a person, by intentionally putting another in fear of injury,
dishonestly induces that person to hand over property, a valuable security, or anything capable of
being converted into one. The gravamen of the offence lies in the victim's own act of parting with
the property, driven by fear rather than by stealth; the offender never removes the property without
the victim's knowledge, but rather compels a delivery that would not otherwise have occurred.

Robbery, defined under Section 309, is theft or extortion in an aggravated form. Theft escalates
into robbery where, in the course of committing the theft or carrying away the stolen property, the
offender causes death, hurt or wrongful restraint, or instils fear of instant death, hurt or restraint.
Extortion escalates into robbery where the offender achieves the extortion by placing the victim in
fear of instant death, hurt or wrongful restraint, rather than merely fear of some future injury. The
presence of immediacy, force or the threat of force operating at the very moment of the offence is
what separates robbery from its milder counterparts.

Every time a person signs up for a new app or website, they are presented with a privacy policy.
In theory, this document explains how their personal data will be collected, stored, and used. In
practice, researchers have found that the average privacy policy takes roughly thirty-four minutes
to read in full, and that most people click “I agree” without reading a single word. This means that
informed consent — the legal and ethical cornerstone of data collection — is, for most users,
entirely fictitious.

The data collected by technology companies is not merely biographical. It includes behavioural
data: which links a person clicks, how long they linger on a page, what they search for at three in
the morning. Aggregated and processed by algorithms, this data produces accurate profiles of a
person’s mental state, political views, purchasing intentions, and even health conditions. These
profiles are then sold to advertisers, insurance companies, and political campaigns, often without
the user’s meaningful awareness.

Defenders of the current system argue that users receive valuable services for free in exchange for
their data, and that anyone who objects can simply choose not to use the platforms. This argument,
critics respond, ignores the reality that opting out is no longer practically possible for most people:
access to jobs, social relationships, and civic participation now depends on digital platforms in
ways that were unimaginable two decades ago.

The European Union’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), introduced in 2018,
attempted to address this imbalance by granting users rights to access, correct, and delete their
data. Early assessments suggest it has had a meaningful effect in some areas, particularly in
requiring companies to be more explicit about consent. However, critics note that enforcement has

In 2012, scientists Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier published research describing a
molecular tool called CRISPR-Cas9, which can edit DNA with a precision that earlier techniques
could not achieve. The system works by guiding a protein to a specific location in the genome,
where it cuts the DNA strand, allowing researchers to delete, correct, or insert genetic material. Its
relative simplicity and low cost triggered what many researchers described as a revolution in
biomedical science, and the two scientists were jointly awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in
2020.

The medical potential is substantial. Diseases caused by a single faulty gene — such as sickle cell
anaemia and cystic fibrosis — are now realistic targets for CRISPR-based therapies. In 2023, the
United Kingdom became the first country to approve a CRISPR treatment for sickle cell disease,
offering patients who previously faced a lifetime of painful episodes a potential functional cure.
Clinical trials for several other conditions are underway in multiple countries.

However, the same technology that corrects a faulty gene in an adult patient’s cells can also be
applied to embryos, potentially altering every cell in a future person’s body, including their
reproductive cells — meaning such edits could be inherited by future generations. In 2018, Chinese
scientist He Jiankui announced he had used CRISPR to edit embryos that were then carried to
term, producing the first gene-edited human babies. The global scientific community’s response
was swift and near-unanimous: the experiment was condemned as premature, unsafe, and ethically
unacceptable, and He Jiankui was subsequently sentenced to prison in China.

Ethicists draw a critical distinction between somatic gene editing — altering cells in a living
patient, with effects confined to that individual — and germline editing, which modifies eggs,
sperm, or embryos and produces heritable changes. Most regulatory bodies consider somatic
